title: Output-layer backpropagation
description: Derive sigmoid/BCE delta, calculate every output gradient, and verify sensitivity with a target-flip practice.
source_short: Backpropagation handout / PDF pp.2-3, sections4-5.2 / original N3.4 network
source: Backpropagation_Derivation.pdf pages 2-3, sections 4-5.2; numerical-practice.md N3.4 and N3.6.

pages.title: Start from the saved forward pass
pages.subtitle: Keep the original parameters from Lessons16-17 fixed throughout backpropagation.
blocks: Our goal is all three output-parameter gradients: how sensitive this one example loss is to each parameter when the others stay fixed.
The handout calls its per-example loss L. We write ell to keep it distinct from a later batch mean J.

pages.title: Delta measures sensitivity to preactivation
pages.subtitle: The backward calculation follows the same dependencies as the forward calculation.

blocks.eq: \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial w}=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}=\delta\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}

blocks: Delta is a derivative with respect to z. A weight gradient is a derivative with respect to a weight. They are connected by the chain rule but are not usually the same number.
First calculate delta at the output; then multiply by each source activation to get that connection gradient. The bias has constant source activation 1.

pages.title: Differentiate binary cross-entropy
pages.subtitle: Handout page 2, section 4.2; assume 0 < y < 1.
blocks: The plus sign in the second term comes from two negatives: the loss has a minus sign and the derivative of (1-y) is -1.

pages.title: Cancel the sigmoid derivative once
pages.subtitle: Handout page 2, section 5.1: this shortcut needs sigmoid output and BCE loss.
blocks: Do not multiply by y(1-y) again after using delta = y-t. That sigmoid factor has already cancelled.
This is a per-example derivative. There is no division by the number of examples here. We will average parameter gradients once in the batch lesson.

pages.title: Check both factors numerically
pages.subtitle: Target t = 1 means the BCE derivative with respect to y is -1/y.
blocks: The two routes agree. Negative delta means a tiny increase in this output preactivation decreases this example loss locally.

pages.title: First output weight: use its source activation
pages.subtitle: Handout page 3, section 5.2. The source is hidden-layer-2 neuron 1.
blocks: The source activation multiplies the weight in the forward weighted sum. That is why it becomes the local derivative with respect to the weight.
Use the activation 0.5627638384, not the hidden preactivation 0.2523866055.

pages.title: Second output weight: keep its own source
pages.subtitle: This connection starts at hidden-layer-2 neuron 2.
blocks: The current weight is -0.4, but this derivative uses its source activation, not the weight itself. The weight will matter when propagating a derivative back to the source neuron.
Keep the original -0.4 for the hidden-layer calculation in Lesson19. Do not update it yet.

pages.title: Output bias: the source is constant one
pages.subtitle: Adding one unit to the bias adds one unit to the preactivation.
blocks: The bias gradient equals delta because its multiplier is 1. This equality does not hold for the other two weight gradients.

pages.title: What does a negative gradient predict?
pages.subtitle: Diagnostic experiment: vary only the output bias; this is not a training update.
blocks: The local estimate is close, not exact, for a finite perturbation. All other weights and biases are held fixed.
Return the bias to its original 0.2. Backpropagation in Lesson19 continues from the original parameter state and forward cache.
Central finite-difference checks of all three output gradients agree with the analytic results.

pages.title: Your turn: flip only the known target
pages.subtitle: Use the same original input (1,2), parameters and forward prediction; set t = 0.
blocks: 1. Explain which forward quantities change when only the target changes.
2. Calculate BCE, the output delta and all three output-parameter gradients.
3. Explain the sign of the bias gradient using a tiny positive bias change with every other parameter fixed.
Do not update any parameters. This is the target-flip retry from numerical-practice N3.6.

pages.title: Practice answer: prediction stays the same
pages.subtitle: Targets enter the loss; this feedforward model does not use them as inputs.
blocks: All forward z and y values remain unchanged. The target changes the loss and the backward derivatives. Positive delta means increasing z locally increases the loss for target zero.

pages.title: Practice answer: all three output gradients
pages.subtitle: Use the same two hidden activations and the new positive delta.
blocks: A tiny positive bias change now increases the loss: it raises the probability of class 1 when the known target is 0.
Checklist: distinguish delta from a weight gradient, use source activations, cancel sigmoid only once, and keep every parameter unchanged until all required gradients are ready.
